archetype.name: Rebuilding (young QB, leaky defense)
archetype.definition: A team in the second year of Kellen Moore's tenure, building around Tyler Shough's passing while the roster around him sits in the bottom third of the league in efficiency, with no run game and a defense that no longer holds up.

report.headline: Passing game is real; turnovers, no run game and a soft defense sink it
report.take:
New Orleans is 3-6, and that is about what it has earned. The point differential implies 3.7 wins, and Wins Over Expected is a modest -0.66. Net EPA ranks 26th, with the offense 22nd and the defense 23rd. This is not an unlucky good team. It is a below-average team that has played below-average football almost every week. The history explains the setting: after five wins in 2024 and six in 2025, the long slide from the 2018-2020 contenders is still running. Tyler Shough has started every game, so whatever this is, it is his team.

The offense is the encouraging part. It scores 23.1 points a game, up from 18 in 2025. Moore is willing to throw, with a pass rate over expected that ranks 10th. Until now the line has protected well, allowing pressure at the 9th-lowest rate. Chris Olave is the clear focal point with 87 targets. Two things have capped it. The run game is broken: a 3.29 yards-per-carry average and a run success rate that ranks 31st, with backs getting only 2.11 yards before contact, which points at the blocking rather than the runners. Then there are the giveaways: 17 offensive turnovers in nine games and a turnover differential of -8. Several of those turnovers came in bunches (three at Detroit, four against Las Vegas, three against Minnesota) and wrecked otherwise competitive games.

The defense is the bigger change. In 2025 it ranked 10th in EPA allowed. Now it ranks 23rd: 28th in success rate allowed, 28th on third down, and 31st in EPA allowed on deep passes. The sack total (23, ranked 10th) hides how little it gets home. Its pressure rate is 31st, so the sacks come from turning a rare pressure into a sack at a high rate, and that tends to fade. The defense has steadied since Atlanta hung 45 on it in Week 4, and nobody has scored more than 27 since. That is partly because it bends in the red zone, where it allows touchdowns at the 11th-best rate. It is still a unit that lets offenses move the ball.

Where it goes from here depends heavily on the offensive line, and the news is bad. Taliese Fuaga and Erik McCoy, both near-every-snap starters, are out. Asim Richards is out for multiple weeks after the Carolina loss. Pass protection was the one structural strength, and it now gets tested against Chicago, Cincinnati and Green Bay in a row. The back half is softer: Arizona, Atlanta, Carolina and two Tampa Bay games. That is where a 5- or 6-win finish comes from, if the turnovers calm down.

strengths.title: Clean pocket, willing passing game
strengths.body: Moore leans on the pass more than the situation calls for, and until last week the line gave Shough time, with pressure and sack rates both in the better half of the league. That is why the offense scores at a league-average clip despite a dead run game. It lasts only as long as the line holds together, and three starters are now out.

strengths.title: Aggressive and effective on short yardage
strengths.body: New Orleans has gone for it on fourth down more readily than anyone, and it converts short-yardage plays at a top-four rate. The run game fails on early downs but finds a push when it needs one yard. That is a coaching edge that should hold, though a patched-up interior line without McCoy will strain it.

strengths.title: Disciplined, and stingy near the goal line
strengths.body: The Saints rarely beat themselves with flags, and the line in particular is among the cleanest units in the league. On defense, the red zone is where the unit finally tightens. It is the main reason the scoreboard hasn't been worse given how freely opponents move between the 20s. Discipline usually holds. Red-zone defense is noisier and is propping up the points-allowed number.

concerns.title: Turnovers are deciding games
concerns.body: Seventeen giveaways in nine games is the single biggest gap between this team and a .500 one. Multi-turnover games against Detroit, Las Vegas and Minnesota turned close games into losses. Some of this should regress toward normal, since turnover rates are erratic. But a young quarterback behind a now-depleted line is the profile where it can get worse before it gets better.

concerns.title: The run game is a line problem
concerns.body: Backs get little before contact, and only a third of runs succeed, a 31st-ranked rate. Both Kendre Miller and Alvin Kamara have the same issue, which points at the blocking. The Carolina game was the low point, with a rushing EPA of -11.9. With two tackles and the center out, there is no reason to expect a fix soon.

concerns.title: A defense with no pass rush
concerns.body: The front barely pressures the quarterback, and the back end gives up the big play, with deep-pass EPA allowed among the league's worst. The result is a 28th-ranked third-down defense that keeps opponents on the field. The healthy sack total comes from converting rare pressures at a high rate, and that tends to fade. Losing rotational DT Christen Miller to injured reserve doesn't help.

trend.note: After the 45-point loss to Atlanta, the defense stopped bleeding, but the offense sputtered, managing 18 rushing yards against Pittsburgh and a deeply negative run game against Carolina. The last month has been a run of one-score games that look a lot like the team's overall level: close, but not good enough.

nextGame.headline: A depleted line meets Chicago's pass rush in Soldier Field
nextGame.body:
Chicago is 7-2, but it is a better team than New Orleans, not a juggernaut. Its Wins Over Expected of 2 ranks 4th, and it is also giving the ball away, with a turnover margin that ranks 29th. Still, it ranks 9th in net EPA, holds the ball longer than anyone, and has the league's best third-down defense along with a top-three sack rate. Its defense smothers the short passing game. The one crack is deep: Chicago ranks last in EPA allowed on deep throws. That is the specific door the Saints need Shough and Olave to walk through. Caleb Williams has started the last six games for the Bears.

Availability tilts this further. New Orleans is without both starting-caliber tackles in Fuaga and Richards and without center McCoy, against a pass rush that already finishes plays. Linebacker Pete Werner is questionable with a hamstring. Chicago's secondary is thinned too: corner Malik Muhammad II is out and Tyrique Stevenson Sr. is questionable. Chicago has lost left tackle Braxton Jones for the year, Luther Burden III is questionable after a concussion, and back Kyle Monangai is aiming to return. The early forecast calls for wind around 16 mph with gusts in the mid-20s. If that holds, it would cut into the deep passing game the Saints most need, so treat it as a hedge, not a given. The Book has Chicago -11.5 with a total of 49.5, and the Saints are +470.

waysToWin.title: Attack Chicago's deep coverage
waysToWin.body: Chicago allows the worst deep-pass EPA in the league and may be missing two corners. Olave, with his 87 targets, is the obvious weapon. Two or three explosive completions are worth more here than any sustained drive against a defense this good on third down. It requires the patched line to hold up just long enough on play-action, and the wind not to cooperate with Chicago.

waysToWin.title: Win the giveaway battle for once
waysToWin.body: Chicago's record runs well ahead of its turnover margin, so the Bears have been coughing it up and surviving. An underdog this size usually needs extra possessions. If the Saints' defense can steal two and Shough plays clean, the game shrinks. That is a big if for a team with 17 giveaways of its own.

waysToWin.title: Get the ball to the lead back
waysToWin.body: Chicago has been soft against opposing lead backs, both in fantasy output over their norm and in EPA a play, where it ranks near the bottom. With protection compromised, quick throws to Kamara, who has 35 targets, act as the run game and the hot read at once. That keeps Shough out of long-developing sacks.

waysToLose.title: The patched line collapses
waysToLose.body: Chicago sacks quarterbacks at a top-three rate and gets off the field on third down better than anyone. New Orleans is missing two tackles and its center, who were nearly every-snap starters. Long-yardage situations behind backups are where Shough's turnovers have come from, and where this game could get away early.

waysToLose.title: Chicago owns the clock
waysToLose.body: The Bears lead the league in time of possession and move the ball well. New Orleans can't get off the field on third down or generate pressure. Long Chicago drives shorten the game and take the Saints' best counter, deep shots, off the table.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden yardage
waysToLose.body: Chicago's special teams rank 4th in EPA a game and New Orleans' rank 24th. In a game where the Saints need everything to break right, giving away field position on kicks makes an 11.5-point gap wider, and gusty wind would magnify kicking edges.

nextGame.watch: Shough's first few long-developing dropbacks behind the replacement tackles and center: if he gets time to test Chicago's last-ranked deep defense, this stays competitive, and if he's sacked or rushed into mistakes, it won't.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule splits cleanly. Chicago, Cincinnati and Green Bay come first, with the offensive line at its thinnest, and that stretch could easily go winless. The last five weeks are against division rivals and Arizona, all with losing or near-.500 records, and that is where the remaining wins are. Tampa Bay twice is a problem for this offense given the Bucs' second-ranked defense. Arizona's 31st-ranked defense and Atlanta's sputtering offense are the softest spots.

What holds up: a pass-first offense that scores in the low 20s when healthy, and a coach who stays aggressive on fourth down. What should regress: the high sack conversion on minimal pressure, which will drag the defense further down. Turnovers should come down somewhat, which helps the offense. The run game is unlikely to improve with this line. Expect a finish in line with the last two seasons rather than a push for the division, even though nobody in the NFC South is above .500.
swingFactors: Results in the four division games

confidence.note: Nine games with one starting QB, but major line injuries change the offense going forward.
